extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, educated readers interested in poetic theory and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging, writing, and criticizing lyrical/romantic poetry, with attention to style, intention, reader-response, and the distinction between imaginative faculties. Draws on examples from Wordsworth, Southey, and contemporary reviewing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge by isolated or accidental failures
rubrics_metrics.description: I know nothing that surpasses the vileness of deciding on the merits of a poet or painter,—(not by characteristic defects; for where there is genius, these always point to his characteristic beauties; but)—by accidental failures or faulty passages; except the impudence of defending it, as the proper duty, and most instructive part, of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selecting and reprinting single bad passages as the basis for condemning an entire author; critics who quote an author’s worst lines (e.g., knitting-needles in Raphael’s backgrounds) waste the reader’s and public’s attention and distort judgment. Treat sporadic failures as such rather than as proof of general incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support criticism by fixed canons deduced from human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: till reviews are conducted on far other principles, and with far other motives; till in the place of arbitrary dictation and petulant sneers, the reviewers support their decisions by reference to fixed canons of criticism, previously established and deduced from the nature of man;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should appeal to established, philosophically grounded standards (not personal whim or satire). Reviewers should justify judgments with reference to consistent critical principles rather than arbitrary taste or malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out and elucidate the beauties of a work
rubrics_metrics.description: He, who points out and elucidates the beauties of an original work does indeed give me interesting information, such as experience would not have authorized me in anticipating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical writing is most valuable when it highlights and explains an author’s strengths; merely telling the reader what is defective gives little new information and is less instructive than exposition of merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the author's stated intentions when judging style
rubrics_metrics.description: The humbler passages in the poems themselves were dwelt on and cited to justify the rejection of the theory. What in and for themselves would have been either forgotten or forgiven as imperfections, or at least comparative failures, provoked direct hostility when announced as intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author has declared a deliberate stylistic choice (e.g., intentional simplicity), critics should evaluate those passages in light of that intention instead of treating them as accidental faults or evidence of perversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination from fancy as separate faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated meditations led me first to suspect ... that Fancy and Imagination were two distinct and widely different faculties, instead of being, according to the general belief, either two names with one meaning, or, at furthest, the lower and higher degree of one and the same power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the nomenclature and theoretical distinction: reserve 'imagination' for the higher, integrating faculty (Milton), and 'fancy' for the more associative/ornamental faculty (Cowley). This distinction should inform both philosophical criticism and poetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the union of deep feeling with profound thought
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying, the objects observed; and above all the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere, and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high poetic excellence combines genuine emotion with intellectual depth, balances truthful observation and imaginative transformation, and establishes an encompassing tone or atmosphere around subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary obscurity and contorted diction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the form, style, and manner of the whole poem ... there is a harshness and acerbity ... The language is not only peculiar and strong, but at times knotty and contorted ... It not seldom therefore justified the complaint of obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While vigor and novelty of expression are valuable, poets should avoid phrasing that is needlessly knotty or contorted so as to demand more close attention than poetry ought to require; undue obscurity is a legitimate ground for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for developmental faults in early works of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic Psyche, in its process to full development, undergoes as many changes ... it is remarkable how soon genius clears and purifies itself from the faults and errors of its earliest products ... faults which ... constitute the very ferment, by which themselves are carried off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should recognise that many defects in early work are transient and part of an artist's maturation; harsh lifelong condemnation for early errors misunderstands the developmental nature of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let minor inferior pieces overshadow a body of work
rubrics_metrics.description: the poems, therefore, at the worst, could only be regarded as so many light or inferior coins in a rouleau of gold, not as so much alloy in a weight of bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat lesser or playful pieces as minor items in a larger oeuvre rather than as contaminating the whole; a collection’s few trifles should not be treated as alloy that devalues the author’s major achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary that small weak passages invite disproportionate attack
rubrics_metrics.description: if in a volume of poetry the critic should find poem or passage which he deems more especially worthless, he is sure to select and reprint it in the review; by which ... he wastes as much more paper than the author ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be mindful that even a few careless lines can become the fulcrum of extended critical hostility; conversely, critics should not allow such passages to determine the overall verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value versatility across poetic forms and species
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry he has attempted almost every species of composition known before, and he has added new ones; ... from the political song ... to the wild ballad; from epistolary ease and graceful narrative, to austere and impetuous moral declamation ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet’s successful engagement with many forms—from political songs and ballads to epic and moral declamation—is a sign of breadth and strength; versatility should be counted positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity and mastery of language and metre as marks of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: been characterized ... but by greater splendour, a deeper pathos, profounder reflections, and a more sustained dignity of language and of metre? ... he has surpassed himself in language and metre, in the construction of the whole, and in the splendour of particular passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained dignity of diction and control of metre across passages and the whole structure of a work are central technical criteria when assessing poetic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the poet’s moral character, industry, and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: his almost unexampled felicity, to possess the best gifts of talent and genius free from all their characteristic defects ... the poet’s matchless industry and perseverance ... The regular and methodical tenor of his daily labours ... loses all semblance of formality in the dignified simplicity of his manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical virtues—steadfast industry, moral probity, reliability, and temperate character—are relevant to a full appraisal of an author’s place and influence (especially in biographical or encomiastic criticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should be principled, not petulant or arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: till in the place of arbitrary dictation and petulant sneers, the reviewers support their decisions by reference to fixed canons of criticism ... reflecting minds will pronounce it arrogance in them thus to announce themselves to men of letters, as the guides of their taste and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers ought to avoid petulance, enmity, or arrogance; principled, well-argued criticism is the proper stance, rather than sneering dictation or appeals to prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reader diversity and prior expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A careful and repeated examination of these confirms me in the belief, that the omission of less than a hundred lines would have precluded nine-tenths of the criticism ... on the supposition, that the reader has taken it up, as he would have done any other collection ... without knowledge of, or reference to, the author’s peculiar opinions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical reception depends on readers’ prior knowledge, tastes, and habits; critics should be mindful of how audience background shapes response, and authors should understand which readers their work will likely reach.
